title: Bell's palsy (adult)
subject: neurology
setting: Emergency department, primary care, ENT and neurology clinic
summary: Sudden unilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness with no other cause: give prednisolone within 72 hours of onset, consider an antiviral only together with the steroid, protect the eye if closure is incomplete, avoid routine tests or imaging, and refer if red flags or no recovery by 3 months.

sections.title: Confirm Bell's palsy
items: Sudden unilateral facial weakness developing over hours to a peak within about 72 hours, involving the forehead (cannot raise the eyebrow or fully close the eye), often with ear or postauricular pain, altered taste or hyperacusis.
About 70% of facial nerve palsies are Bell's palsy, so examine all cranial nerves, limbs, ears, parotid glands and the skin of the head and face to exclude another cause.
Grade severity (House-Brackmann I to VI) and note whether paralysis is complete; complete paralysis recovers less well.
More common in pregnancy, diabetes and after upper respiratory infection.

sections.title: Red flags: consider another cause
items: Forehead sparing, limb weakness, dysarthria, ataxia or other cranial nerve palsies: think stroke or brainstem lesion and manage as stroke.
Gradual progression over weeks, recurrent palsy on the same side, facial twitching, a parotid mass or skin cancer of the face or scalp: suspect a tumour and arrange MRI.
Vesicles in the ear canal or on the palate, severe ear pain, hearing loss or vertigo: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster); give an antiviral plus steroid and refer to ENT.
Ear discharge, fever, hearing loss or cholesteatoma: otitis media or mastoiditis; urgent ENT review.
Bilateral palsy: consider Guillain-Barré syndrome, sarcoidosis, Lyme disease in endemic areas, HIV, leukaemia and leprosy.

sections.title: Treatment within 72 hours
items: Age 16 or over and within 72 hours of onset: prescribe oral prednisolone (AAO-HNS strong recommendation): 50 mg once daily for 10 days, or 60 mg once daily for 5 days then reduce by 10 mg a day over 5 days.
Benefit of starting steroids after 72 hours is unclear.

Do not give an antiviral alone. An antiviral may be added to the steroid within 72 hours after shared decision-making; any benefit is small and unproven (valaciclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days, or aciclovir 400 mg five times daily for 10 days).
Diabetes and pregnancy were excluded from the trials: decide individually. Steroids are usually still given in diabetes, with closer glucose monitoring.
Do not order routine blood tests, imaging or electrodiagnostic tests for typical Bell's palsy.

sections.title: Eye care
items: Incomplete eye closure: lubricating eye drops through the day and eye ointment at night; glasses or goggles outdoors.
Taping the eyelid closed or a moisture chamber at night helps, but teach the technique, because poorly applied tape or patches can abrade the cornea.
Eye pain, redness, irritation or blurred vision: urgent ophthalmology review for exposure keratopathy.

sections.title: Follow-up and prognosis
items: Most recover: in the Scottish trial, 94% given early prednisolone had recovered at 9 months, compared with 82% without it.
Reassess or refer to a facial nerve specialist for new or worsening neurological signs, eye symptoms at any time, or incomplete recovery at 3 months.
No recovery by 3 months: MRI of the whole facial nerve course with gadolinium to exclude a tumour.
Complete paralysis: electrodiagnostic testing may be offered, usually in specialist care.
Long-term problems (synkinesis, contracture, crocodile tears, lagophthalmos): refer for facial therapy or eyelid procedures such as a gold weight or botulinum toxin.

sections.title: Special groups
items: Pregnancy: more common in the third trimester; decide on steroids individually with obstetric input, and check blood pressure and urine.
Under 16: spontaneous recovery is better and evidence for steroids is inconclusive; steroids may be considered after discussion with carers.
India: consider leprosy (anaesthetic skin patches, thickened nerves), tuberculous otitis media and HIV infection, especially if the palsy is atypical, bilateral or recurrent.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Missing a stroke because forehead movement was not tested.
Missing Ramsay Hunt syndrome by not examining the ear and mouth.
Delaying prednisolone for investigations.
Prescribing an antiviral without a steroid.
Forgetting eye protection, leading to corneal ulceration.

drugs.name: Prednisolone
drugs.dose: 50 mg orally once daily for 10 days; or 60 mg once daily for 5 days, then reduce by 10 mg daily over 5 days
drugs.notes: Start within 72 hours of onset. Monitor glucose in diabetes; consider gastroprotection if other risk factors.

drugs.name: Valaciclovir
drugs.dose: 1 g orally three times daily for 7 days, only together with prednisolone
drugs.notes: Optional; reduce dose in renal impairment. For Ramsay Hunt syndrome see Herpes zoster (shingles), adult.

drugs.name: Aciclovir
drugs.dose: 400 mg orally five times daily for 10 days, only together with prednisolone
drugs.notes: Alternative to valaciclovir; reduce dose in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Ocular lubricants
drugs.dose: Lubricating eye drops frequently by day and eye ointment at night to the affected eye
